note: "Alun-alun" refers to a traditional public town square, common in Javanese cities; often the social and civic center of a town.

sentences.text: Kami bermain di alun-alun kota.
sentences.en: We are playing at the town square.

sentences.text: Alun-alun itu sangat ramai hari ini.
sentences.en: The town square is very crowded today.

sentences.text: Saya suka jalan-jalan di alun-alun.
sentences.en: I like to walk around the town square.

english: the head of a regency or a, sub-provincial district
note: 'Bupati' is a formal/official title for a regional district head, similar to a county executive; often seen with the prefix 'Pak' or 'Bu' as a sign of respect.

sentences.text: Bupati membuka acara festival budaya hari ini.
sentences.en: The district head opens the cultural festival today.

sentences.text: Pak bupati tinggal di kantor kabupaten.
sentences.en: The district head lives at the regency office.

sentences.text: Kami bertemu bupati di balai desa.
sentences.en: We met the district head at the village hall.

note: 'Desa' refers to a village as an official administrative unit in Indonesia; more formal than 'kampung' (neighborhood/hometown).

sentences.text: Saya tinggal di desa yang kecil.
sentences.en: I live in a small village.

sentences.text: Desa ini sangat indah dan tenang.
sentences.en: This village is very beautiful and peaceful.

sentences.text: Nenek saya lahir di desa.
sentences.en: My grandmother was born in a village.

note: 'Kampung' means village or hometown; often used warmly to refer to one's home village, distinct from 'desa' which is more formal/administrative.

sentences.text: Saya tinggal di kampung yang kecil.
sentences.en: I live in a small village.

sentences.text: Kampung saya ada di Bali.
sentences.en: My village is in Bali.

sentences.text: Anak-anak bermain di kampung itu.
sentences.en: The children are playing in that village.

note: 'Kebun' means garden or plantation; commonly used in phrases like 'kebun binatang' (zoo) and 'kebun sayur' (vegetable garden); not to be confused with 'taman' which refers to a decorative park.

sentences.text: Ibu menanam bunga di kebun.
sentences.en: Mother plants flowers in the garden.

sentences.text: Kebun sayur kami sangat besar.
sentences.en: Our vegetable garden is very big.

sentences.text: Ayah bekerja di kebun setiap pagi.
sentences.en: Father works in the garden every morning.

note: 'Kelas' means both a physical classroom and a grade/year level in school; very common in everyday school contexts.

sentences.text: Saya belajar di kelas dua.
sentences.en: I study in grade two.

sentences.text: Kelas kami bersih dan nyaman.
sentences.en: Our classroom is clean and comfortable.

sentences.text: Ibu guru masuk ke kelas.
sentences.en: The teacher enters the classroom.

note: 'Kue' refers broadly to cakes, pastries, and sweet snacks; very common in daily life; related words: 'kue ulang tahun' (birthday cake), 'kue basah' (moist traditional snack).

sentences.text: Ibu membuat kue untuk ulang tahun saya.
sentences.en: Mom makes a cake for my birthday.

sentences.text: Saya makan kue di warung tadi.
sentences.en: I ate a cake at the stall earlier.

sentences.text: Kue ini sangat manis dan enak.
sentences.en: This cake is very sweet and delicious.

note: 'Meja' means table; common in daily life; related words: 'kursi' (chair), 'meja makan' (dining table), 'meja tulis' (desk).

sentences.text: Ada buku di atas meja.
sentences.en: There is a book on the table.

sentences.text: Kami makan di meja bersama.
sentences.en: We eat at the table together.

sentences.text: Tolong taruh piring di meja.
sentences.en: Please put the plate on the table.

english: a small boat, a traditional Indonesian, sailboat, a yacht
note: 'Perahu' refers to a small traditional boat, often seen on rivers, lakes, or coastal areas in Indonesia; do not confuse with 'kapal' which is a larger ship or vessel.

sentences.text: Saya naik perahu di danau itu.
sentences.en: I ride a small boat on that lake.

sentences.text: Perahu itu berwarna merah dan putih.
sentences.en: That small boat is red and white.

sentences.text: Nelayan itu punya perahu kecil.
sentences.en: That fisherman has a small boat.

note: 'Pertandingan' means a competitive match or game (sports); related: 'permainan' (game/play), 'kompetisi' (competition); commonly used for football, badminton, and other sports.

sentences.text: Pertandingan sepak bola itu sangat seru.
sentences.en: That football match was very exciting.

sentences.text: Kami menonton pertandingan bola bersama teman.
sentences.en: We watched a football match with friends.

sentences.text: Kapan pertandingan badminton itu mulai?
sentences.en: When does the badminton match start?

note: 'Pesta' means a party or festival; more festive/large-scale than 'perayaan'; commonly used for birthday parties ('pesta ulang tahun') and community celebrations.

sentences.text: Kami pergi ke pesta ulang tahun Budi.
sentences.en: We went to Budi's birthday party.

sentences.text: Pesta di desa itu sangat meriah.
sentences.en: The festival in that village is very lively.

sentences.text: Saya suka makan di pesta keluarga.
sentences.en: I like eating at family parties.

english: an island, the island of Bali
note: 'Pulau' means 'island'; when used as a proper name prefix (e.g., Pulau Bali), it is capitalized, similar to saying 'the island of Bali'.

sentences.text: Saya ingin pergi ke Pulau Bali.
sentences.en: I want to go to the island of Bali.

sentences.text: Indonesia mempunyai banyak pulau yang indah.
sentences.en: Indonesia has many beautiful islands.

sentences.text: Pulau Bali sangat terkenal di dunia.
sentences.en: The island of Bali is very famous in the world.

note: 'Sayuran' is the general word for vegetables (collective/plural); a single vegetable type is often just named directly (e.g., 'wortel' for carrot); related: 'buah' (fruit), 'makanan' (food).

sentences.text: Ibu membeli sayuran di pasar pagi.
sentences.en: Mom buys vegetables at the morning market.

sentences.text: Saya suka makan sayuran setiap hari.
sentences.en: I like to eat vegetables every day.

sentences.text: Sayuran ini sangat segar dan murah.
sentences.en: These vegetables are very fresh and cheap.

note: "Sepak bola" is the standard term for soccer/football in Indonesia; "bola" alone can mean any ball, so use the full phrase to be specific.

sentences.text: Anak-anak bermain sepak bola di lapangan.
sentences.en: The children are playing football in the field.

sentences.text: Saya suka menonton sepak bola bersama teman.
sentences.en: I like watching football with friends.

sentences.text: Sepak bola adalah olahraga populer di Indonesia.
sentences.en: Football is a popular sport in Indonesia.

note: 'Sungai' means river; commonly confused with 'danau' (lake) or 'laut' (sea); used in everyday speech across Indonesia.

sentences.text: Anak-anak bermain di sungai setiap hari.
sentences.en: The children play in the river every day.

sentences.text: Sungai ini sangat panjang dan indah.
sentences.en: This river is very long and beautiful.

sentences.text: Kami melihat ikan di sungai itu.
sentences.en: We saw fish in that river.

note: '-belas' is the suffix added to numbers 11–19 (e.g., 'sebelas'=11, 'dua belas'=12, 'tiga belas'=13); note that 11 is 'sebelas' (not 'satu belas').

sentences.text: Saya berumur empat belas tahun.
sentences.en: I am fourteen years old.

sentences.text: Ada lima belas siswa di kelas.
sentences.en: There are fifteen students in the class.

sentences.text: Toko itu tutup jam tujuh belas.
sentences.en: The shop closes at seventeen o'clock.

english: how much, how many, what (when asking about a, number)
note: "Berapa" is used in questions about numbers, prices, ages, and quantities; often paired with "harga" (price) or "umur" (age); very common in markets and daily transactions.

sentences.text: Berapa harga nasi goreng ini?
sentences.en: How much does this fried rice cost?

sentences.text: Kamu berapa tahun sekarang?
sentences.en: How old are you now?

sentences.text: Ada berapa orang di sini?
sentences.en: How many people are here?

note: 'Delapan' means eight; it is a standalone cardinal number — related words include 'kedelapan' (eighth/the eighth) and 'delapan belas' (eighteen).

sentences.text: Saya punya delapan ekor ayam di rumah.
sentences.en: I have eight chickens at home.

sentences.text: Toko itu buka jam delapan pagi.
sentences.en: That shop opens at eight in the morning.

sentences.text: Ada delapan siswa di kelas ini.
sentences.en: There are eight students in this class.

note: 'Dua' means 'two'; used for counting and quantities; related words: 'kedua' (second/both), 'dua kali' (twice).

sentences.text: Saya punya dua kucing di rumah.
sentences.en: I have two cats at home.

sentences.text: Dia memesan dua kopi pagi ini.
sentences.en: She ordered two coffees this morning.

sentences.text: Ada dua anak bermain di pantai.
sentences.en: There are two children playing on the beach.

note: 'Enam' means 'six' and is used for counting; remember it differs from 'delapan' (eight) and 'tujuh' (seven), which beginners often mix up.

sentences.text: Saya punya enam ekor ayam di rumah.
sentences.en: I have six chickens at home.

sentences.text: Warung itu buka jam enam pagi.
sentences.en: That food stall opens at six in the morning.

sentences.text: Ada enam kursi di meja makan.
sentences.en: There are six chairs at the dining table.

note: 'Empat' means four; used in counting, age, time, and prices; related: 'keempat' (fourth), 'empat belas' (fourteen).

sentences.text: Saya punya empat ekor kucing di rumah.
sentences.en: I have four cats at home.

sentences.text: Toko itu buka jam empat sore.
sentences.en: That shop opens at four in the afternoon.

sentences.text: Dia membeli empat buah mangga di pasar.
sentences.en: She bought four mangoes at the market.

note: 'Ibu' means 'Mrs' or 'mother'; used as a respectful title for older women; often shortened to 'Bu' in casual speech.

sentences.text: Ibu guru mengajar di kelas hari ini.
sentences.en: The teacher (Mrs) is teaching in class today.

sentences.text: Selamat pagi, Ibu!
sentences.en: Good morning, Mrs!

sentences.text: Ibu membeli sayur di pasar.
sentences.en: The lady (Mrs) is buying vegetables at the market.

note: KTP is the Indonesian national identity card; always use the acronym in everyday speech, not the full form.

sentences.text: Saya perlu membawa KTP ke kantor.
sentences.en: I need to bring my identity card to the office.

sentences.text: Tolong tunjukkan KTP Anda kepada saya.
sentences.en: Please show me your identity card.

sentences.text: KTP saya hilang kemarin.
sentences.en: My identity card was lost yesterday.

note: 'Lima' means 'five' and is used in counting, prices, and telling time; do not confuse with 'lemon' or 'limau' (citrus fruit).

sentences.text: Saya punya lima ekor kucing di rumah.
sentences.en: I have five cats at home.

sentences.text: Toko itu buka jam lima sore.
sentences.en: The shop opens at five in the afternoon.

sentences.text: Dia membeli lima mangga di pasar.
sentences.en: She bought five mangoes at the market.

note: "Nol" is the standard word for zero in Indonesian, used in numbers, scores, and temperatures; also heard as the digit '0' when reading phone numbers or codes.

sentences.text: Suhu hari ini nol derajat di sana.
sentences.en: The temperature there is zero degrees today.

sentences.text: Nilai ujiannya nol karena tidak hadir.
sentences.en: His exam score is zero because he did not attend.

sentences.text: Nomor teleponnya dimulai dari nol delapan.
sentences.en: His phone number starts with zero eight.

english: number (such-and-such), such-and-such a number, in room number 6
note: "Nomor" means "number" when referring to a specific number (room, phone, ticket, etc.); often abbreviated "No." in writing; not used for counting quantities (use "angka" for digits or "jumlah" for amounts).

sentences.text: Kamar saya nomor enam.
sentences.en: My room is number six.

sentences.text: Nomor telepon saya mudah diingat.
sentences.en: My phone number is easy to remember.

sentences.text: Tiket saya nomor dua puluh.
sentences.en: My ticket is number twenty.

english: the number-word, indicating multiples of ten, thirty
note: 'Puluh' is a suffix/word used with numbers to mean multiples of ten (e.g., tiga puluh = thirty, lima puluh = fifty); never used alone for a single ten — use 'sepuluh' for ten.

sentences.text: Harga ini tiga puluh ribu rupiah.
sentences.en: This price is thirty thousand rupiah.

sentences.text: Ada dua puluh siswa di kelas.
sentences.en: There are twenty students in the class.

sentences.text: Saya punya lima puluh ribu rupiah.
sentences.en: I have fifty thousand rupiah.

note: "Satu" means "one" (the number); also used in "satu-satu" (one by one) and combined in numbers like "dua puluh satu" (twenty-one); not to be confused with "pertama" (first/ordinal).

sentences.text: Saya mau pesan satu nasi goreng.
sentences.en: I want to order one fried rice.

sentences.text: Ada satu kucing di taman.
sentences.en: There is one cat in the park.

sentences.text: Dia punya satu adik perempuan.
sentences.en: She has one younger sister.

note: 'Sebelas' means eleven; part of the basic number series (satu, dua, tiga...), commonly used for time, age, and counting.

sentences.text: Saya bangun jam sebelas pagi.
sentences.en: I wake up at eleven in the morning.

sentences.text: Ada sebelas orang di warung itu.
sentences.en: There are eleven people at that food stall.

sentences.text: Adik saya umur sebelas tahun.
sentences.en: My younger sibling is eleven years old.

note: 'Sepuluh' means 'ten' and is used in everyday counting, prices, and time; combine with 'ribu' (thousand) for prices like 'sepuluh ribu' (ten thousand rupiah).

sentences.text: Saya punya sepuluh ekor ayam di rumah.
sentences.en: I have ten chickens at home.

sentences.text: Harga jeruk ini sepuluh ribu rupiah.
sentences.en: The price of these oranges is ten thousand rupiah.

sentences.text: Kami mulai belajar jam sepuluh pagi.
sentences.en: We start studying at ten in the morning.

note: The prefix 'se-' means 'one' or 'a/an' when attached to a number or noun (e.g., seratus = one hundred, semangkok = a bowl); avoid confusing it with the suffix '-se' in other languages.

sentences.text: Saya mau beli semangkok nasi goreng.
sentences.en: I want to buy a bowl of fried rice.

sentences.text: Dia punya seratus ribu rupiah.
sentences.en: He has one hundred thousand rupiah.

sentences.text: Tolong beri saya segelas air putih.
sentences.en: Please give me a glass of water.

note: 'Seorang' is used as 'a/one' specifically for people (humans only); use 'seekor' for animals and 'sebuah' for objects.

sentences.text: Dia adalah seorang guru yang baik.
sentences.en: She is a good teacher.

sentences.text: Saya bertemu seorang teman di pasar.
sentences.en: I met a friend at the market.

sentences.text: Ada seorang dokter di klinik itu.
sentences.en: There is a doctor at that clinic.

note: 'Telepon' means telephone/phone call; also used as a verb meaning 'to call'; related: 'menelepon' (to telephone someone), 'telepon genggam' (mobile phone).

sentences.text: Saya punya satu telepon di rumah.
sentences.en: I have one telephone at home.

sentences.text: Telepon saya ada di meja.
sentences.en: My telephone is on the table.

sentences.text: Ibu mau telepon nenek sekarang.
sentences.en: Mom wants to call grandma now.

note: 'Tiga' means 'three' and is used for counting; related words include 'ketiga' (third/the three of) and 'bertiga' (together as three people).

sentences.text: Saya punya tiga kucing di rumah.
sentences.en: I have three cats at home.

sentences.text: Kami memesan tiga nasi goreng untuk makan.
sentences.en: We ordered three fried rice for the meal.

sentences.text: Toko itu tutup jam tiga sore.
sentences.en: That shop closes at three in the afternoon.

note: 'Tujuh' means seven; part of the basic number set, often confused with 'tujuan' (destination/goal) which sounds similar.

sentences.text: Saya punya tujuh ekor ayam di rumah.
sentences.en: I have seven chickens at home.

sentences.text: Toko itu buka jam tujuh pagi.
sentences.en: That shop opens at seven in the morning.

sentences.text: Dia membeli tujuh buah mangga.
sentences.en: He bought seven mangoes.

note: 'Jumlah' means sum, total, or quantity; often confused with 'nomor' (a specific number/ID) — use 'jumlah' for counted amounts or totals.

sentences.text: Jumlah siswa di kelas ini dua puluh.
sentences.en: The number of students in this class is twenty.

sentences.text: Berapa jumlah uang di dompet kamu?
sentences.en: How much money is in your wallet?

sentences.text: Jumlah apel di meja ada lima.
sentences.en: The total number of apples on the table is five.

note: 'Rupiah' is the official Indonesian currency (IDR); commonly abbreviated as 'Rp', used in all cash and price contexts.

sentences.text: Harga ini sepuluh ribu rupiah.
sentences.en: This price is ten thousand rupiah.

sentences.text: Saya punya lima puluh ribu rupiah.
sentences.en: I have fifty thousand rupiah.

sentences.text: Berapa rupiah harga nasi goreng ini?
sentences.en: How many rupiah does this fried rice cost?

note: "Sama dengan" means "equals" in math contexts; don't confuse with "sama" alone meaning "same/with" in everyday speech.

sentences.text: Dua tambah dua sama dengan empat.
sentences.en: Two plus two equals four.

sentences.text: Lima kurang tiga sama dengan dua.
sentences.en: Five minus three equals two.

sentences.text: Sepuluh dibagi dua sama dengan lima.
sentences.en: Ten divided by two equals five.

note: 'Seratus' means one hundred; combine with other numbers like 'seratus lima puluh' (150); used for prices, counting, and quantities in everyday speech.

sentences.text: Harga kopi ini seratus ribu rupiah.
sentences.en: The price of this coffee is one hundred thousand rupiah.

sentences.text: Saya punya seratus teman di sekolah.
sentences.en: I have one hundred friends at school.

sentences.text: Nenek membeli seratus telur di pasar.
sentences.en: Grandma bought one hundred eggs at the market.

note: "Seribu" means one thousand; often used in prices and counting; related: "ribu" (thousand, used after digits like "dua ribu" = two thousand).

sentences.text: Harga air mineral ini seribu rupiah.
sentences.en: The price of this mineral water is one thousand rupiah.

sentences.text: Saya punya seribu rupiah di saku.
sentences.en: I have one thousand rupiah in my pocket.

sentences.text: Kue ini harganya seribu rupiah saja.
sentences.en: This cake costs only one thousand rupiah.

note: 'Seribu lima ratus' means 1,500; used in markets and shops for prices, combine 'seribu' (1,000) and 'lima ratus' (500).

sentences.text: Harga kopi ini seribu lima ratus rupiah.
sentences.en: The price of this coffee is one thousand five hundred rupiah.

sentences.text: Saya bayar seribu lima ratus untuk air.
sentences.en: I pay one thousand five hundred for water.

sentences.text: Pisang itu seribu lima ratus per buah.
sentences.en: That banana is one thousand five hundred per piece.

note: 'Tambah' means 'plus/add' in math; also used informally to mean 'more' or 'extra' in everyday speech.

sentences.text: Dua tambah tiga sama dengan lima.
sentences.en: Two plus three equals five.

sentences.text: Satu tambah satu adalah dua.
sentences.en: One plus one is two.

sentences.text: Lima tambah empat sama dengan sembilan.
sentences.en: Five plus four equals nine.

note: "Beberapa" means 'several/some' and is used before nouns to indicate an unspecified small number; do not confuse with "sedikit" (a little/few in amount) or "beberapa" with time expressions like "beberapa hari" (a few days).

sentences.text: Saya membeli beberapa buah di pasar.
sentences.en: I bought some fruit at the market.

sentences.text: Ada beberapa orang di pantai itu.
sentences.en: There are several people on that beach.

sentences.text: Dia punya beberapa teman di Bali.
sentences.en: She has some friends in Bali.

english: a tourist bureau, a travel agency
note: 'Biro pariwisata' is the formal/written term for a travel agency; in casual speech Indonesians often just say 'agen travel' or 'agen wisata'.

sentences.text: Saya pergi ke biro pariwisata kemarin.
sentences.en: I went to the travel agency yesterday.

sentences.text: Biro pariwisata itu jual tiket pesawat.
sentences.en: That travel agency sells plane tickets.

sentences.text: Kami pesan tur di biro pariwisata.
sentences.en: We booked a tour at the travel agency.

note: "Dalam" means 'in/inside/within'; commonly confused with 'di dalam' (more emphatic 'inside'); related: 'di dalam' (inside), 'dalam hati' (in the heart)

sentences.text: Buku itu ada dalam tas saya.
sentences.en: The book is in my bag.

sentences.text: Dia tinggal dalam rumah yang besar.
sentences.en: She lives in a big house.

sentences.text: Ada apa dalam kotak itu?
sentences.en: What is in that box?

note: 'Gambar' means picture/image/drawing; related words: 'menggambar' (to draw), 'foto' (photo); used for both drawings and printed images.

sentences.text: Saya suka gambar kucing itu.
sentences.en: I like that picture of a cat.

sentences.text: Anak itu menunjuk gambar di buku.
sentences.en: That child is pointing at a picture in the book.

sentences.text: Ini gambar keluarga saya.
sentences.en: This is a picture of my family.

note: 'Hanya' means 'only/just'; it is interchangeable with 'saja' but placed before the word it limits, not after.

sentences.text: Saya hanya minum air putih setiap hari.
sentences.en: I only drink plain water every day.

sentences.text: Di warung itu hanya ada nasi goreng.
sentences.en: At that small restaurant there is only fried rice.

sentences.text: Dia hanya punya satu buku.
sentences.en: She only has one book.

note: 'Kendaraan' is a neutral, everyday word for any vehicle (car, bike, etc.); related words: 'mobil' (car), 'motor' (motorbike), 'naik kendaraan' means 'to ride/take a vehicle'.

sentences.text: Kendaraan ini sangat cepat di jalan.
sentences.en: This vehicle is very fast on the road.

sentences.text: Dia punya satu kendaraan di rumah.
sentences.en: He has one vehicle at home.

sentences.text: Kami naik kendaraan ke pasar bersama.
sentences.en: We ride a vehicle to the market together.

note: 'Kilometer' is used the same as in English; Indonesians often shorten it to 'km' in writing, and it is used for road distances and travel.

sentences.text: Jarak rumah saya dua kilometer dari sini.
sentences.en: My house is two kilometres from here.

sentences.text: Sekolah itu lima kilometer dari pasar.
sentences.en: That school is five kilometres from the market.

sentences.text: Kami berjalan satu kilometer ke pantai.
sentences.en: We walked one kilometre to the beach.

note: "Kira-kira" means 'approximately' or 'about'; often confused with "kira" alone which means 'to think/guess'; related to "sekitar" (around/about).

sentences.text: Harga ini kira-kira dua puluh ribu rupiah.
sentences.en: This price is about twenty thousand rupiah.

sentences.text: Pantai itu kira-kira dua kilometer dari sini.
sentences.en: That beach is roughly two kilometers from here.

sentences.text: Dia kira-kira berumur tiga puluh tahun.
sentences.en: She is approximately thirty years old.

english: a sort, a kind, a sort of, a kind of
note: "Macam" is informal/colloquial for 'kind/sort/type'; often interchangeable with "jenis" but more casual; also used in "macam-macam" meaning 'various/all kinds of'.

sentences.text: Ada banyak macam buah di pasar.
sentences.en: There are many kinds of fruit at the market.

sentences.text: Saya suka macam-macam makanan Indonesia.
sentences.en: I like all kinds of Indonesian food.

sentences.text: Ini macam apa?
sentences.en: What kind is this?

note: 'Stasiun' refers to a train station; for bus terminals use 'terminal', and for police stations use 'kantor polisi'.

sentences.text: Saya pergi ke stasiun naik taksi.
sentences.en: I go to the station by taxi.

sentences.text: Kereta berangkat dari stasiun jam tujuh.
sentences.en: The train departs from the station at seven o'clock.

sentences.text: Di mana stasiun kereta terdekat?
sentences.en: Where is the nearest train station?

note: 'Truk' is an informal loanword from English 'truck'; commonly used in everyday speech alongside the formal 'kendaraan berat'.

sentences.text: Truk itu membawa banyak buah segar.
sentences.en: That truck is carrying a lot of fresh fruit.

sentences.text: Ada truk besar di jalan raya.
sentences.en: There is a big truck on the highway.

sentences.text: Ayah melihat truk merah di pasar.
sentences.en: Father saw a red truck at the market.

note: 'Betul' means correct or right; similar to 'benar' but more casual and commonly used in everyday speech.

sentences.text: Ya, betul sekali! Kamu pintar.
sentences.en: Yes, that's exactly right! You are smart.

sentences.text: Jawaban kamu betul.
sentences.en: Your answer is correct.

sentences.text: Itu betul, terima kasih.
sentences.en: That's right, thank you.

english: to be such-and-such an age, to be so many years old
note: 'Berumur' is used in everyday speech to state someone's age; it is interchangeable with 'berusia' (slightly more formal); do not confuse with 'umur' (noun: age) alone.

sentences.text: Adik saya berumur tujuh tahun sekarang.
sentences.en: My younger sibling is seven years old now.

sentences.text: Kucing itu berumur tiga tahun.
sentences.en: That cat is three years old.

sentences.text: Nenek saya berumur tujuh puluh tahun.
sentences.en: My grandmother is seventy years old.

english: If that's the case..., If that's how things stand...
note: "Kalau begitu" is a casual spoken phrase used to draw a conclusion or make a decision based on what was just said; similar to "jadi" but more conversational.

sentences.text: Kalau begitu, kita pergi sekarang saja.
sentences.en: If that's the case, let's just go now.

sentences.text: Kalau begitu, saya pesan nasi goreng.
sentences.en: If that's how it is, I'll order fried rice.

sentences.text: Kalau begitu, kamu istirahat dulu ya.
sentences.en: If that's the case, you should rest first.

note: 'Lahir' means 'to be born' and is used in everyday speech; commonly seen in 'tanggal lahir' (date of birth) and 'tempat lahir' (place of birth).

sentences.text: Saya lahir di Bali pada tahun 2000.
sentences.en: I was born in Bali in the year 2000.

sentences.text: Adik saya lahir di rumah sakit.
sentences.en: My younger sibling was born in the hospital.

sentences.text: Kapan kamu lahir?
sentences.en: When were you born?

english: to begin, to start, to make a beginning
note: 'Mulai' means 'to start/begin' and is used before verbs or alone; often paired with 'dari' (from) as 'mulai dari'; do not confuse with 'memulai' (to initiate something), which is more formal.

sentences.text: Kelas bahasa Indonesia mulai jam delapan.
sentences.en: The Indonesian class starts at eight o'clock.

sentences.text: Ayo kita mulai makan sekarang.
sentences.en: Let's start eating now.

sentences.text: Hujan mulai turun sore ini.
sentences.en: The rain starts to fall this afternoon.

note: Formal noun used for any president; often followed by a name (e.g., 'Presiden Jokowi'); same form for singular and plural, no article needed.

sentences.text: Presiden tinggal di Jakarta.
sentences.en: The president lives in Jakarta.

sentences.text: Saya melihat foto Presiden di kantor.
sentences.en: I saw a photo of the president at the office.

sentences.text: Presiden berbicara di televisi tadi malam.
sentences.en: The president spoke on television last night.

note: "Pada" means 'on/at/in' and is used for time, dates, and formal location; often interchangeable with 'di' for place but more formal.

sentences.text: Saya bangun pada pukul enam pagi.
sentences.en: I wake up at six in the morning.

sentences.text: Pada hari Minggu, kami pergi ke pantai.
sentences.en: On Sunday, we go to the beach.

sentences.text: Acara dimulai pada malam ini.
sentences.en: The event starts tonight.

english: a primary school, an elementary school
note: "Sekolah dasar" (often abbreviated as "SD") refers to primary/elementary school for ages 6–12; do not confuse with "sekolah menengah" (middle/high school).

sentences.text: Adik saya pergi ke sekolah dasar.
sentences.en: My younger sibling goes to primary school.

sentences.text: Sekolah dasar itu dekat rumah saya.
sentences.en: That primary school is near my house.

sentences.text: Saya belajar di sekolah dasar dulu.
sentences.en: I used to study at primary school.

note: 'Tahun' means 'year'; use it for age (tahun ini = this year), and note 'bulan' means 'month' — a common mix-up for beginners.

sentences.text: Saya tinggal di Bali dua tahun.
sentences.en: I have lived in Bali for two years.

sentences.text: Tahun ini saya belajar bahasa Indonesia.
sentences.en: This year I am learning Indonesian.

sentences.text: Dia berumur dua puluh tahun.
sentences.en: She is twenty years old.

note: "Tahun berapa?" means "what year?" and is used to ask about a specific year; often heard alongside "kapan" (when) but more specific to year.

sentences.text: Kamu lahir tahun berapa?
sentences.en: What year were you born?

sentences.text: Bali dikunjungi tahun berapa?
sentences.en: What year did you visit Bali?

sentences.text: Sekolah ini dibangun tahun berapa?
sentences.en: What year was this school built?

english: someone's age, how old someone is
note: 'Umur' means age or how old someone is; often interchangeable with 'usia' but 'umur' is more casual and everyday.

sentences.text: Berapa umur kamu sekarang?
sentences.en: How old are you now?

sentences.text: Umur saya dua puluh tahun.
sentences.en: My age is twenty years old.

sentences.text: Dia tidak tahu umur neneknya.
sentences.en: He does not know his grandmother's age.

english: a younger brother or sister, someone's younger sibling
note: "Adik" refers to any younger sibling regardless of gender; use "kakak" for an older sibling; often shortened to "dik" in casual speech.

sentences.text: Adik saya suka makan nasi goreng.
sentences.en: My younger sibling likes to eat fried rice.

sentences.text: Saya pergi ke sekolah dengan adik.
sentences.en: I go to school with my younger sibling.

sentences.text: Adik saya bermain di taman.
sentences.en: My younger sibling is playing in the park.

note: 'Anak' means child or son/daughter; used in everyday speech; related words include 'anak-anak' (children) and 'anak laki-laki' (son).

sentences.text: Saya punya satu anak perempuan.
sentences.en: I have one daughter.

sentences.text: Anak itu bermain di taman.
sentences.en: The child is playing in the park.

sentences.text: Ibu membeli baju untuk anak.
sentences.en: Mom bought clothes for the child.

note: 'Ayah' is the standard/formal word for father; 'bapak' or 'papa' are also common, with 'papa' being more informal.

sentences.text: Ayah saya bekerja di kantor setiap hari.
sentences.en: My father works at the office every day.

sentences.text: Saya pergi ke pasar dengan ayah.
sentences.en: I go to the market with my father.

sentences.text: Ayah memasak nasi goreng untuk kami.
sentences.en: Father cooks fried rice for us.

note: 'Bekerja' is a formal/neutral verb meaning 'to work'; in casual speech Indonesians often say 'kerja' instead; related: 'pekerjaan' (job/work), 'pekerja' (worker).

sentences.text: Ayah saya bekerja di kantor setiap hari.
sentences.en: My father works at the office every day.

sentences.text: Dia bekerja di restoran dekat pantai.
sentences.en: She works at a restaurant near the beach.

sentences.text: Saya ingin bekerja di Bali.
sentences.en: I want to work in Bali.

note: 'Dia' is used for both 'he/she/him/her' in Indonesian; there is no gender distinction, making it simpler than English pronouns.

sentences.text: Dia makan nasi goreng setiap pagi.
sentences.en: He/She eats fried rice every morning.

sentences.text: Saya suka dia karena dia baik.
sentences.en: I like him/her because he/she is kind.

sentences.text: Dia pergi ke pantai hari ini.
sentences.en: He/She is going to the beach today.

note: "Istri" means wife in a neutral/formal register; the informal equivalent is "bini"; related words include "suami" (husband) and "menikah" (to marry).

sentences.text: Istri saya memasak nasi goreng setiap pagi.
sentences.en: My wife cooks fried rice every morning.

sentences.text: Dia pergi ke pasar dengan istri.
sentences.en: He goes to the market with his wife.

sentences.text: Suami dan istri itu tinggal di Bali.
sentences.en: That husband and wife live in Bali.

english: an older brother or sister, someone's older sibling
note: 'Kakak' is an informal, friendly title for an older sibling or any older person; often shortened to 'Kak' when addressing someone directly.

sentences.text: Kakak saya suka makan nasi goreng.
sentences.en: My older sibling likes to eat fried rice.

sentences.text: Di mana kakak sekarang?
sentences.en: Where is your older sibling now?

sentences.text: Kakak pergi ke pasar pagi ini.
sentences.en: My older sibling went to the market this morning.

note: 'Kakek' means grandfather; the informal form is 'kek'; often paired with 'nenek' (grandmother).

sentences.text: Kakek saya suka minum kopi setiap pagi.
sentences.en: My grandfather likes to drink coffee every morning.

sentences.text: Saya pergi ke rumah kakek kemarin.
sentences.en: I went to my grandfather's house yesterday.

sentences.text: Kakek dan nenek tinggal di Bali.
sentences.en: Grandfather and grandmother live in Bali.

note: 'Keluarga' means 'family' as a group; use 'anggota keluarga' for 'family member'; common in everyday and formal speech.

sentences.text: Saya tinggal bersama keluarga saya di Bali.
sentences.en: I live with my family in Bali.

sentences.text: Keluarga saya makan bersama setiap malam.
sentences.en: My family eats together every night.

sentences.text: Kami pergi ke pantai dengan keluarga.
sentences.en: We go to the beach with family.

note: 'Laki-laki' means male/man and is the standard neutral term; 'pria' is slightly more formal, while 'cowok' is informal slang.

sentences.text: Anak laki-laki itu bermain di pantai.
sentences.en: That boy is playing at the beach.

sentences.text: Dia adalah laki-laki yang baik.
sentences.en: He is a good man.

sentences.text: Satu laki-laki duduk di warung.
sentences.en: One man is sitting at the food stall.

english: by the name of..., whose name is..., his/her/its name is...
note: "namanya" means 'his/her/its/their name is' or 'by the name of'; formed from "nama" (name) + "-nya" (possessive/topic suffix); commonly used to introduce people, animals, or things by name.

sentences.text: Saya punya kucing, namanya Putih.
sentences.en: I have a cat; its name is Putih.

sentences.text: Ini teman saya, namanya Budi.
sentences.en: This is my friend, his name is Budi.

sentences.text: Ada warung di sini, namanya Warung Sari.
sentences.en: There is a small restaurant here, by the name of Warung Sari.

note: 'Nenek' means grandmother; used as both a title and a term of address, similar to calling her 'Grandma' directly; related word: 'kakek' (grandfather).

sentences.text: Nenek saya tinggal di Bali.
sentences.en: My grandmother lives in Bali.

sentences.text: Saya makan nasi dengan nenek.
sentences.en: I eat rice with my grandmother.

sentences.text: Nenek memasak sayur di dapur.
sentences.en: Grandmother cooks vegetables in the kitchen.

note: '-nya' attaches to nouns to mean 'his/her/its'; also used as 'the' for definiteness, e.g. 'rumahnya' = 'his/her house' or 'the house'.

sentences.text: Namanya Budi dan dia dari Bali.
sentences.en: His name is Budi and he is from Bali.

sentences.text: Saya suka rumahnya karena besar.
sentences.en: I like her house because it is big.

sentences.text: Anjingnya sangat lucu dan kecil.
sentences.en: His/her dog is very cute and small.

note: 'Orang tua' literally means 'old person' but is the standard word for 'parents'; use 'orang tua saya' for 'my parents'.

sentences.text: Orang tua saya tinggal di Bali.
sentences.en: My parents live in Bali.

sentences.text: Saya pergi dengan orang tua saya.
sentences.en: I go with my parents.

sentences.text: Orang tua saya suka masak nasi.
sentences.en: My parents like to cook rice.

note: 'Pacar' is the everyday informal word for boyfriend or girlfriend; more formal alternatives include 'kekasih' or 'pasangan'.

sentences.text: Dia adalah pacar saya yang baru.
sentences.en: He/She is my new boyfriend/girlfriend.

sentences.text: Pacar saya tinggal di Bali.
sentences.en: My boyfriend/girlfriend lives in Bali.

sentences.text: Kami pergi makan dengan pacar kami.
sentences.en: We went to eat with our boyfriends/girlfriends.

note: "Perempuan" means female/woman; more formal than "cewek" (informal), and distinct from "wanita" which is slightly more polite/formal; used for girls and women of any age.

sentences.text: Perempuan itu membeli nasi di pasar.
sentences.en: That woman is buying rice at the market.

sentences.text: Dia adalah perempuan yang baik.
sentences.en: She is a good woman.

sentences.text: Ada dua perempuan di warung itu.
sentences.en: There are two women at that food stall.

note: 'Punya' means 'to have/own'; used informally in everyday speech, more casual than 'memiliki'; also used as a possessive marker (e.g., 'punya saya' = 'mine').

sentences.text: Saya punya satu kucing di rumah.
sentences.en: I have one cat at home.

sentences.text: Dia punya banyak teman di Bali.
sentences.en: She has many friends in Bali.

sentences.text: Kamu punya uang untuk beli nasi?
sentences.en: Do you have money to buy rice?

english: a brother/sister, a sibling, a relative
note: "Saudara" means sibling or relative; also used as a formal/polite 'you' when addressing strangers.

sentences.text: Saya punya satu saudara di Bali.
sentences.en: I have one sibling in Bali.

sentences.text: Saudara saya tinggal di Jakarta.
sentences.en: My sibling lives in Jakarta.

sentences.text: Apakah saudara kamu sudah makan?
sentences.en: Has your sibling eaten yet?

note: 'Suami' means husband; the female equivalent is 'istri' (wife); commonly used in everyday formal and informal speech.

sentences.text: Suami saya bekerja di kantor setiap hari.
sentences.en: My husband works at the office every day.

sentences.text: Di mana suami kamu sekarang?
sentences.en: Where is your husband now?

sentences.text: Suami saya suka makan nasi goreng.
sentences.en: My husband likes to eat fried rice.

note: "Tentang" means "about" or "concerning" and is used before a topic; beginners often confuse it with "sekitar" (around/approximately), but "tentang" is strictly for topics, not locations or quantities.

sentences.text: Saya belajar tentang budaya Bali.
sentences.en: I am learning about Balinese culture.

sentences.text: Dia bercerita tentang keluarganya.
sentences.en: She is talking about her family.

sentences.text: Buku ini tentang masakan Indonesia.
sentences.en: This book is about Indonesian food.

note: 'Aja' is the informal/colloquial form of 'saja' (just/only), very common in everyday spoken Indonesian; avoid in formal writing.

sentences.text: Minum air aja, jangan minum kopi.
sentences.en: Just drink water, don't drink coffee.

sentences.text: Saya mau nasi goreng aja.
sentences.en: I just want fried rice.

sentences.text: Tunggu di sini aja, ya.
sentences.en: Just wait here, okay.

note: "Ama" is an informal/colloquial substitute for "dengan" (with); common in casual speech and texting, especially among younger Indonesians, but avoid in formal writing.

sentences.text: Aku pergi ke pasar ama ibu.
sentences.en: I went to the market with mom.

sentences.text: Dia makan siang ama temannya.
sentences.en: She had lunch with her friend.

sentences.text: Saya beli oleh-oleh ama adik.
sentences.en: I bought souvenirs together with my younger sibling.

english: or [when you are stressing, an 'either/or' contrast], (informal/slangy)
note: Used informally to stress an 'either/or' choice, stronger/more emphatic than 'atau'; common in casual speech and slang, especially in questions.

sentences.text: Kamu mau nasi apa mie?
sentences.en: Do you want rice or noodles?

sentences.text: Dia pergi apa tidak?
sentences.en: Did he go or not?

sentences.text: Kamu suka kopi apa teh?
sentences.en: Do you like coffee or tea?

note: 'Belum' means 'not yet' and is used instead of 'tidak' when something hasn't happened but may happen later; opposite is 'sudah' (already).

sentences.text: Saya belum makan pagi ini.
sentences.en: I have not eaten breakfast yet today.

sentences.text: Dia belum datang ke warung.
sentences.en: She has not come to the food stall yet.

sentences.text: Kami belum pesan kopi.
sentences.en: We have not ordered coffee yet.

note: "Bilang" is a casual, spoken alternative to "mengatakan" or "berkata"; common in everyday speech but avoid in formal writing.

sentences.text: Dia bilang mau pergi ke pasar.
sentences.en: She said she wants to go to the market.

sentences.text: Ibu bilang makan dulu sebelum pergi.
sentences.en: Mom said to eat first before leaving.

sentences.text: Kamu bilang apa tadi?
sentences.en: What did you say just now?

note: 'Cakep' is informal/colloquial for attractive or good-looking; used for people, and sometimes things; similar to 'ganteng' (for males) or 'cantik' (for females) but more casual and gender-neutral.

sentences.text: Wah, kamu cakep sekali hari ini!
sentences.en: Wow, you look really good-looking today!

sentences.text: Dia cakep dan baik hati.
sentences.en: She/He is attractive and kind-hearted.

sentences.text: Baju baru kamu cakep banget.
sentences.en: Your new clothes look really nice.

english: pretty, beautiful, (describing the appearance, of girls/women)
note: "Cantik" describes beauty/prettiness for girls and women; for men use "tampan" or "ganteng"; closely related to "indah" which describes scenery or objects.

sentences.text: Adik perempuan saya sangat cantik.
sentences.en: My younger sister is very pretty.

sentences.text: Baju itu cantik sekali.
sentences.en: That dress is very beautiful.

sentences.text: Ibu saya cantik dan baik hati.
sentences.en: My mother is beautiful and kind.

note: "Duit" is a very common informal/colloquial word for money; more casual than "uang" (the standard word), used freely in everyday speech but avoid in formal writing.

sentences.text: Aku tidak punya duit sekarang.
sentences.en: I don't have any money right now.

sentences.text: Berapa duit harga nasi goreng ini?
sentences.en: How much money does this fried rice cost?

sentences.text: Dia simpan duit di dalam tas.
sentences.en: She keeps her money inside her bag.

note: "Gimana" is an informal/colloquial form of "bagaimana" (how/what is ... like); very common in everyday speech but avoid in formal writing.

sentences.text: Gimana liburanmu di Bali kemarin?
sentences.en: How was your holiday in Bali yesterday?

sentences.text: Gimana rasanya nasi goreng ini?
sentences.en: What does this fried rice taste like?

sentences.text: Gimana cuaca di sana sekarang?
sentences.en: What is the weather like there now?

note: 'Kawin' means 'to get married' and is common in everyday speech, though 'menikah' is more formal; do not confuse with 'kawin' used for animals in biological contexts.

sentences.text: Kakak saya akan kawin bulan depan.
sentences.en: My older sibling will get married next month.

sentences.text: Mereka kawin di Bali tahun lalu.
sentences.en: They got married in Bali last year.

sentences.text: Kapan kamu mau kawin?
sentences.en: When do you want to get married?

note: "Kerja" is the informal/everyday word for 'to work' or 'work'; the more formal term is "bekerja", but "kerja" is far more common in casual speech.

sentences.text: Saya kerja di toko setiap hari.
sentences.en: I work at the shop every day.

sentences.text: Dia kerja dari pagi sampai sore.
sentences.en: She works from morning until afternoon.

sentences.text: Kamu kerja di mana sekarang?
sentences.en: Where do you work now?

note: "Masih" means "still" (ongoing state); don't confuse with "sudah" (already) or "lagi" (again/more).

sentences.text: Saya masih belajar bahasa Indonesia.
sentences.en: I am still learning Indonesian.

sentences.text: Dia masih tidur di kamar.
sentences.en: He/She is still sleeping in the room.

sentences.text: Kopi ini masih panas.
sentences.en: This coffee is still hot.

note: 'Muda' means young (person) or unripe (fruit); don't confuse with 'mudah' meaning easy.

sentences.text: Dia sangat muda dan cantik.
sentences.en: She is very young and beautiful.

sentences.text: Anak muda itu suka berselancar di Bali.
sentences.en: That young person likes to surf in Bali.

sentences.text: Ibu saya masih terlihat muda.
sentences.en: My mother still looks young.

note: 'Ortu' is an informal abbreviation of 'orang tua' (parents); common in casual speech and texting among young Indonesians, avoid in formal situations.

sentences.text: Ortu saya tinggal di Bali.
sentences.en: My parents live in Bali.

sentences.text: Saya pergi ke pasar dengan ortu.
sentences.en: I go to the market with my parents.

sentences.text: Ortu aku sangat baik hati.
sentences.en: My parents are very kind.

note: 'Sudah' means 'already' and is also used to indicate a completed action; often paired with verbs, and sometimes confused with 'telah' which is more formal.

sentences.text: Saya sudah makan nasi goreng tadi.
sentences.en: I already ate fried rice just now.

sentences.text: Dia sudah pergi ke pantai.
sentences.en: She has already gone to the beach.

sentences.text: Kami sudah beli oleh-oleh di pasar.
sentences.en: We already bought souvenirs at the market.

note: "Tanggal" means a specific calendar date; don't confuse it with "hari" (day of the week) or "bulan" (month).

sentences.text: Hari ini tanggal berapa?
sentences.en: What is today's date?

sentences.text: Ulang tahun saya tanggal dua puluh.
sentences.en: My birthday is on the twentieth.

sentences.text: Kelas mulai tanggal satu Januari.
sentences.en: Class starts on the first of January.

note: 'Terkenal' means famous or well-known; similar to 'populer' but 'terkenal' implies wider recognition; often used for places, people, and food.

sentences.text: Restoran ini terkenal karena ayam gorengnya.
sentences.en: This restaurant is famous for its fried chicken.

sentences.text: Bali terkenal dengan pantainya yang indah.
sentences.en: Bali is famous for its beautiful beaches.

sentences.text: Dia adalah penyanyi terkenal di Indonesia.
sentences.en: She is a famous singer in Indonesia.

note: 'Teman' means friend in a casual, everyday register; 'sahabat' is a closer/best friend, and 'kawan' is a slightly more informal synonym.

sentences.text: Saya pergi ke pantai dengan teman saya.
sentences.en: I go to the beach with my friend.

sentences.text: Teman saya suka makan nasi goreng.
sentences.en: My friend likes to eat fried rice.

sentences.text: Kami bermain bola dengan teman baru.
sentences.en: We play ball with a new friend.

note: 'Tua' means old (for people or things); opposite is 'muda' (young); do not confuse with 'lama' which means old in the sense of 'a long time ago'.

sentences.text: Kakek saya sudah sangat tua.
sentences.en: My grandfather is already very old.

sentences.text: Pohon ini tua dan besar.
sentences.en: This tree is old and big.

sentences.text: Nenek tua itu tersenyum ramah.
sentences.en: That old grandmother smiled kindly.

note: "tuh" is a very casual spoken form of "itu" (that/those); used in informal speech and texting, avoid in formal or written contexts.

sentences.text: Siapa tuh yang datang ke sini?
sentences.en: Who is that coming here?

sentences.text: Beli nasi goreng tuh enak banget.
sentences.en: That fried rice you bought is really delicious.

sentences.text: Tuh, kucing di depan rumah.
sentences.en: There, a cat is in front of the house.

note: 'Uang' is the everyday word for money; 'duit' is a casual synonym, while 'harga' means price — do not confuse them.

sentences.text: Saya tidak punya uang sekarang.
sentences.en: I don't have money right now.

sentences.text: Berapa uang untuk tiket ini?
sentences.en: How much money is for this ticket?

sentences.text: Dia menyimpan uang di dompet.
sentences.en: She keeps money in her wallet.

note: 'Udah' is informal/colloquial for 'sudah' (already); very common in everyday speech but avoid in formal writing.

sentences.text: Aku udah makan nasi goreng tadi.
sentences.en: I already ate fried rice just now.

sentences.text: Dia udah pergi ke pantai.
sentences.en: She already went to the beach.

sentences.text: Kamu udah minum air hari ini?
sentences.en: Have you already drunk water today?

english: oh! ouch!, (an exclamation of pain, shock or surprise)
note: "Aduh!" is a very common, informal exclamation used to express pain, surprise, or frustration; similar to "ouch!", "oh no!", or "oh my!" in English.

sentences.text: Aduh! Kakiku sakit sekali!
sentences.en: Ouch! My foot really hurts!

sentences.text: Aduh, aku lupa bawa uang!
sentences.en: Oh no, I forgot to bring money!

sentences.text: Aduh! Air ini sangat panas!
sentences.en: Ouch! This water is very hot!

note: 'Alamat' means address (home, email, etc.); also informally used to mean 'a sign of something coming' but stick to the address meaning as a beginner.

sentences.text: Apa alamat rumah kamu?
sentences.en: What is your home address?

sentences.text: Tolong tulis alamat kamu di sini.
sentences.en: Please write your address here.

sentences.text: Saya tidak tahu alamat hotel itu.
sentences.en: I don't know the address of that hotel.

note: "Agama" means religion in general; commonly seen on Indonesian ID cards (KTP) listing one of the six official religions; related words: beragama (to have a religion), keagamaan (religious affairs).

sentences.text: Agama saya adalah Islam.
sentences.en: My religion is Islam.

sentences.text: Di Indonesia ada banyak agama.
sentences.en: In Indonesia there are many religions.

sentences.text: Apa agama kamu?
sentences.en: What is your religion?

english: to help someone, to assist someone
note: "Bantu" is informal and very common; use "membantu" in formal writing; often paired with "tolong" for polite requests.

sentences.text: Bisa kamu bantu saya membawa tas ini?
sentences.en: Can you help me carry this bag?

sentences.text: Saya mau bantu ibu di dapur.
sentences.en: I want to help mom in the kitchen.

sentences.text: Dia selalu bantu teman-temannya belajar.
sentences.en: She always helps her friends study.

english: to go to school, (i.e. to be enrolled at a school)
note: "Bersekolah" means to attend or be enrolled in school; more formal than "sekolah" used as a verb; related: "sekolah" (school/noun), "pergi ke sekolah" (to go to school).

sentences.text: Adik saya bersekolah di Denpasar.
sentences.en: My younger sibling goes to school in Denpasar.

sentences.text: Dia bersekolah setiap hari Senin.
sentences.en: She goes to school every Monday.

sentences.text: Anak itu bersekolah di sini.
sentences.en: That child goes to school here.

note: 'Hidup' means 'to live/to be alive'; also used as an exclamation meaning 'long live!'; related words: 'kehidupan' (life/lifestyle), 'menghidupi' (to support/provide for).

sentences.text: Kakek saya masih hidup dan sehat.
sentences.en: My grandfather is still alive and healthy.

sentences.text: Saya ingin hidup di Bali.
sentences.en: I want to live in Bali.

sentences.text: Semua orang ingin hidup bahagia.
sentences.en: Everyone wants to live happily.

english: to go/come along, to join in, to also do something with, others
note: "Ikut" is informal and very common; use it to say you're joining someone or tagging along, often interchangeable with "ikut serta"; beginners sometimes confuse it with "pergi" (to go alone).

sentences.text: Boleh saya ikut ke pasar?
sentences.en: May I come along to the market?

sentences.text: Dia ikut makan malam bersama kami.
sentences.en: She joined us for dinner.

sentences.text: Anak itu ikut bermain di pantai.
sentences.en: The child joined in playing at the beach.

note: 'Jadi' means 'so/therefore' as a conjunction; don't confuse with its other meaning 'to become' — context tells them apart.

sentences.text: Hujan turun, jadi kita tidak pergi.
sentences.en: It rained, so we didn't go.

sentences.text: Dia lapar, jadi dia makan nasi.
sentences.en: She was hungry, so she ate rice.

sentences.text: Toko tutup, jadi saya pulang.
sentences.en: The shop was closed, so I went home.

english: information, data, a statement/declaration, (concerning the facts of a, matter)
note: "Keterangan" is a formal/neutral noun used for written or spoken information, explanations, or official statements; related to "menerangkan" (to explain) and often seen on forms labeled "keterangan" meaning "description/remarks".

sentences.text: Saya butuh keterangan dari dokter.
sentences.en: I need a statement from the doctor.

sentences.text: Beri keterangan lengkap di formulir ini.
sentences.en: Provide complete information on this form.

sentences.text: Keterangan itu sangat membantu saya.
sentences.en: That information was very helpful to me.

note: 'lagi' is very common in spoken Indonesian; it can mean 'again' (mau lagi = want more/again), 'still' (masih lagi), or 'else' (siapa lagi = who else); often confused with 'lagi' meaning 'still/currently' in informal speech

sentences.text: Saya mau makan nasi goreng lagi.
sentences.en: I want to eat fried rice again.

sentences.text: Tolong ulangi lagi, saya tidak mengerti.
sentences.en: Please repeat again, I don't understand.

sentences.text: Mau minum air lagi tidak?
sentences.en: Do you want more water?

english: to pass away, (a polite way of saying, 'to die')
note: 'Meninggal' is a polite/formal way to say 'to die' in Indonesian; avoid the blunt 'mati' for people, as it is considered rude.

sentences.text: Kakek saya meninggal tahun lalu.
sentences.en: My grandfather passed away last year.

sentences.text: Anjing tua itu meninggal kemarin.
sentences.en: The old dog passed away yesterday.

sentences.text: Nenek meninggal ketika saya masih kecil.
sentences.en: Grandmother passed away when I was still young.

note: "Permisi" is a polite, everyday phrase used to excuse yourself or get someone's attention; more formal than "maaf" for passing by or interrupting.

sentences.text: Permisi, saya mau lewat.
sentences.en: Excuse me, I want to pass.

sentences.text: Permisi, di mana toilet?
sentences.en: Excuse me, where is the toilet?

sentences.text: Permisi, boleh saya masuk?
sentences.en: Excuse me, may I come in?

english: you, Mr, Mrs, Ms, (formal and egalitarian)
note: "Saudara" is a formal, gender-neutral 'you' used in official or polite settings; also means 'sibling/relative'; avoid confusing with casual 'kamu' or 'Anda'.

sentences.text: Apakah Saudara sudah makan hari ini?
sentences.en: Have you eaten today?

sentences.text: Saudara bisa duduk di sini.
sentences.en: You may sit here.

sentences.text: Nama Saudara siapa?
sentences.en: What is your name?

note: Formal term for a senior technical/vocational high school in Indonesia; often abbreviated as STA; distinct from SMK (vocational school) and SMA (general high school).

sentences.text: Adik saya belajar di Sekolah Teknik Atas.
sentences.en: My younger sibling studies at a senior technical high school.

sentences.text: Sekolah Teknik Atas itu dekat pasar.
sentences.en: That senior technical high school is near the market.

sentences.text: Budi ingin masuk Sekolah Teknik Atas.
sentences.en: Budi wants to enter a senior technical high school.

note: "Sudah berapa lama" asks about duration of an ongoing situation; use it before a verb or noun phrase, and don't confuse it with "berapa lama" alone which asks about future or general duration.

sentences.text: Sudah berapa lama kamu tinggal di Bali?
sentences.en: How long have you lived in Bali?

sentences.text: Sudah berapa lama dia belajar bahasa Indonesia?
sentences.en: How long has he/she been studying Indonesian?

sentences.text: Sudah berapa lama kamu kerja di sini?
sentences.en: How long have you worked here?

note: "Tanda tangan" literally means "sign hand"; it refers to a handwritten signature, not a digital one; related: "tanda" (sign/mark), "tangan" (hand).

sentences.text: Tolong beri tanda tangan di sini.
sentences.en: Please give your signature here.

sentences.text: Saya perlu tanda tangan Anda sekarang.
sentences.en: I need your signature now.

sentences.text: Di mana saya harus tanda tangan?
sentences.en: Where do I have to sign?

note: "Atap" means roof or rooftop; commonly used in everyday speech; related words include "langit-langit" (ceiling) and "genteng" (roof tile).

sentences.text: Atap rumah kami bocor saat hujan.
sentences.en: Our house roof leaks when it rains.

sentences.text: Kucing itu duduk di atas atap.
sentences.en: That cat is sitting on the roof.

sentences.text: Kami memperbaiki atap yang rusak kemarin.
sentences.en: We repaired the broken roof yesterday.

note: 'Bagian' means 'part' or 'section'; commonly used for parts of a place, body, or group; related: 'sebagian' (some/part of).

sentences.text: Bagian dapur ada di belakang rumah.
sentences.en: The kitchen area is at the back of the house.

sentences.text: Ini bagian terpenting dari pelajaran ini.
sentences.en: This is the most important part of this lesson.

sentences.text: Saya suka bagian pantai yang tenang.
sentences.en: I like the quiet part of the beach.

note: "Dapur" means kitchen; commonly used in everyday home contexts; related words include "masak" (to cook) and "meja dapur" (kitchen table).

sentences.text: Ibu memasak nasi di dapur.
sentences.en: Mom is cooking rice in the kitchen.

sentences.text: Dapur kami kecil tapi bersih.
sentences.en: Our kitchen is small but clean.

sentences.text: Adik minum air di dapur.
sentences.en: My younger sibling is drinking water in the kitchen.

english: front (when you are talking, about the front part of, something)
note: "Depan" means the front part or front side of something; don't confuse with "muka" (face/front in formal contexts); also used in "di depan" (in front of).

sentences.text: Pintu depan rumah itu berwarna merah.
sentences.en: The front door of that house is red.

sentences.text: Dia duduk di depan kelas.
sentences.en: She sits at the front of the class.

sentences.text: Warung itu ada di depan pasar.
sentences.en: That small restaurant is in front of the market.

note: "Gudang" means a storage room or warehouse; often confused with "toko" (shop) — a gudang stores goods, a toko sells them.

sentences.text: Barang-barang itu ada di gudang.
sentences.en: Those items are in the storeroom.

sentences.text: Pak Budi menyimpan sepeda di gudang.
sentences.en: Mr. Budi keeps his bicycle in the storeroom.

sentences.text: Gudang itu sangat besar.
sentences.en: That warehouse is very big.

english: yard, (i.e. a fenced/walled area, adjacent to a house/building)
note: "Halaman" means a yard or courtyard next to a house/building; also means "page" (of a book), so context matters.

sentences.text: Anak-anak bermain di halaman rumah.
sentences.en: The children are playing in the yard of the house.

sentences.text: Halaman sekolah itu sangat luas.
sentences.en: The school yard is very large.

sentences.text: Ibu menyapu halaman setiap pagi.
sentences.en: Mother sweeps the yard every morning.

note: 'Jendela' means window (the opening in a wall); not to be confused with 'pintu' (door); commonly used in home and classroom contexts.

sentences.text: Tolong buka jendela itu, panas sekali.
sentences.en: Please open that window, it is very hot.

sentences.text: Saya duduk di dekat jendela.
sentences.en: I sit near the window.

sentences.text: Jendela kamar saya menghadap ke taman.
sentences.en: My room's window faces the garden.

note: 'Kamar kecil' is a polite, common term for toilet/restroom; 'toilet' and 'WC' are also widely used in Indonesia.

sentences.text: Di mana kamar kecil di sini?
sentences.en: Where is the restroom here?

sentences.text: Saya perlu ke kamar kecil sekarang.
sentences.en: I need to go to the restroom now.

sentences.text: Kamar kecil ada di sebelah kanan.
sentences.en: The restroom is on the right side.

note: 'Kamar mandi' literally means 'bathing room'; used for any bathroom/toilet in everyday speech, often interchangeable with 'toilet' or 'WC' in informal contexts.

sentences.text: Di mana kamar mandi di sini?
sentences.en: Where is the bathroom here?

sentences.text: Saya mau ke kamar mandi dulu.
sentences.en: I want to go to the bathroom first.

sentences.text: Kamar mandi ada di sebelah kanan.
sentences.en: The bathroom is on the right side.

note: 'Kamar tidur' literally means 'sleep room'; commonly used in everyday speech, distinct from 'kamar mandi' (bathroom).

sentences.text: Kamar tidur saya ada di lantai dua.
sentences.en: My bedroom is on the second floor.

sentences.text: Dia tidur di kamar tidur setiap malam.
sentences.en: He sleeps in the bedroom every night.

sentences.text: Kamar tidur ini sangat bersih dan nyaman.
sentences.en: This bedroom is very clean and comfortable.

note: 'Pagar' means fence or barrier; commonly used for home/garden fences; related words: 'pintu pagar' (gate), 'pagar rumah' (house fence).

sentences.text: Ada pagar tinggi di depan rumah.
sentences.en: There is a tall fence in front of the house.

sentences.text: Anak itu duduk di atas pagar.
sentences.en: That child is sitting on the fence.

sentences.text: Ayah saya membuat pagar dari bambu.
sentences.en: My father makes a fence from bamboo.

note: 'Pohon' means tree; 'kayu' means wood/timber — don't confuse them; plural is the same form: 'pohon-pohon' for multiple trees.

sentences.text: Ada pohon besar di depan rumah.
sentences.en: There is a big tree in front of the house.

sentences.text: Anak itu duduk di bawah pohon.
sentences.en: That child is sitting under the tree.

sentences.text: Pohon ini sangat tinggi.
sentences.en: This tree is very tall.

note: 'Pintu' means door or entrance; 'pintu masuk' = entrance, 'pintu keluar' = exit; not to be confused with 'jendela' (window).

sentences.text: Tolong tutup pintu itu.
sentences.en: Please close that door.

sentences.text: Pintu kamar saya terbuka.
sentences.en: My room door is open.

sentences.text: Di mana pintu masuk hotel ini?
sentences.en: Where is the entrance to this hotel?

note: "Ruang keluarga" literally means "family room" and refers to the main living/lounge area; beginners sometimes confuse it with "ruang tamu" (guest room / formal sitting room for visitors).

sentences.text: Kami menonton TV di ruang keluarga.
sentences.en: We watch TV in the living room.

sentences.text: Sofa baru ada di ruang keluarga.
sentences.en: The new sofa is in the lounge room.

sentences.text: Ibu duduk di ruang keluarga sekarang.
sentences.en: Mum is sitting in the living room now.

note: 'Ruang makan' literally means 'eating room'; commonly used in homes and restaurants, distinct from 'dapur' (kitchen) and 'restoran' (restaurant).

sentences.text: Kami makan malam di ruang makan.
sentences.en: We have dinner in the dining room.

sentences.text: Ruang makan itu bersih dan nyaman.
sentences.en: The dining room is clean and comfortable.

sentences.text: Meja besar ada di ruang makan.
sentences.en: There is a big table in the dining room.

note: 'Ruang tamu' literally means 'guest room' but refers to the living room or reception area where guests are welcomed; not to be confused with 'kamar tamu' (guest bedroom).

sentences.text: Kami duduk di ruang tamu bersama.
sentences.en: We sit together in the living room.

sentences.text: Ada sofa baru di ruang tamu.
sentences.en: There is a new sofa in the living room.

sentences.text: Ibu menyambut tamu di ruang tamu.
sentences.en: Mother welcomes guests in the reception area.

english: guest, visitor, customer (i.e. someone, who comes into a shop)
note: "Tamu" is a neutral, everyday word used for guests at home, hotel visitors, and shop customers; commonly seen in signs like 'Area Tamu' (guest area).

sentences.text: Ada tamu di depan pintu.
sentences.en: There is a guest at the door.

sentences.text: Tamu itu membeli baju di toko.
sentences.en: That customer is buying a shirt at the shop.

sentences.text: Ibu menyambut tamu dengan senyum.
sentences.en: Mother welcomes the guest with a smile.

english: for, (i.e. intended for someone, or something), (in order) to
note: "Untuk" is neutral/everyday and means 'for' (intended for) or 'to/in order to'; don't confuse it with "buat" which is informal and means the same but more colloquial.

sentences.text: Ini kopi untuk kamu.
sentences.en: This coffee is for you.

sentences.text: Saya belajar untuk ujian besok.
sentences.en: I am studying for the exam tomorrow.

sentences.text: Dia pergi ke pasar untuk membeli buah.
sentences.en: She goes to the market to buy fruit.

english: a toilet (room), a toilet bowl, a WC
note: "WC" (pronounced "way-say") is borrowed from Dutch and widely used in Indonesia for both the toilet room and the toilet bowl; more formal than "toilet" but less formal than "kamar mandi".

sentences.text: Di mana WC di sini?
sentences.en: Where is the toilet here?

sentences.text: WC di hotel itu bersih sekali.
sentences.en: The toilet in that hotel is very clean.

sentences.text: Saya perlu ke WC sekarang.
sentences.en: I need to go to the toilet now.

english: to go shopping, to do the shopping
note: "Berbelanja" is a formal/standard form of shopping; casual speech often uses "belanja" alone; related: "pergi belanja" (go shopping), "pasar" (market).

sentences.text: Ibu suka berbelanja di pasar setiap pagi.
sentences.en: Mom likes to go shopping at the market every morning.

sentences.text: Kami berbelanja sayuran di pasar tradisional.
sentences.en: We do the shopping for vegetables at the traditional market.

note: 'Bercakap-cakap' means to have a casual conversation; more formal than 'ngobrol' but both are common; related: 'berbicara' (to speak).

sentences.text: Kami bercakap-cakap di warung setiap pagi.
sentences.en: We chat at the food stall every morning.

sentences.text: Ibu dan tetangga bercakap-cakap di depan rumah.
sentences.en: Mom and the neighbor chat in front of the house.

sentences.text: Saya suka bercakap-cakap dengan teman baru.
sentences.en: I like to chat with new friends.

note: 'Bermain' means 'to play' and is used for games, sports, and instruments; beginners sometimes confuse it with 'main' which is the informal root word.

sentences.text: Anak-anak bermain di taman setiap hari.
sentences.en: The children play in the park every day.

sentences.text: Saya suka bermain bola di pantai.
sentences.en: I like to play ball at the beach.

sentences.text: Mereka bermain musik bersama teman-teman.
sentences.en: They play music together with friends.

note: 'Gaji' means salary or wages; used for regular employment pay, not one-time payments (use 'upah' for daily/task wages); related: 'gaji bulanan' (monthly salary).

sentences.text: Gaji saya dibayar setiap bulan.
sentences.en: My salary is paid every month.

sentences.text: Berapa gaji kamu di tempat kerja?
sentences.en: How much is your salary at work?

sentences.text: Dia senang karena gaji naik.
sentences.en: She is happy because her salary increased.

note: 'ia' means 'he' or 'she' and is slightly more formal than 'dia'; both are common in everyday speech

sentences.text: Ia pergi ke pasar setiap pagi.
sentences.en: She goes to the market every morning.

sentences.text: Ia makan nasi goreng di warung.
sentences.en: He eats fried rice at the food stall.

sentences.text: Ia guru di sekolah ini.
sentences.en: She is a teacher at this school.

note: 'Kaya' means 'rich/wealthy'; do not confuse with 'kaya' meaning 'like/as' in some regional dialects; related words: 'miskin' (poor), 'uang' (money).

sentences.text: Dia sangat kaya dan punya rumah besar.
sentences.en: He is very rich and has a big house.

sentences.text: Keluarga itu kaya karena kerja keras.
sentences.en: That family is rich because of hard work.

sentences.text: Saya ingin kaya suatu hari nanti.
sentences.en: I want to be rich someday.

note: 'Komputer' is a direct loanword from English; used in both formal and informal speech, often interchangeable with 'laptop' in casual conversation.

sentences.text: Saya belajar dengan komputer di rumah.
sentences.en: I study with a computer at home.

sentences.text: Komputer saya rusak hari ini.
sentences.en: My computer is broken today.

sentences.text: Dia membeli komputer baru kemarin.
sentences.en: She bought a new computer yesterday.

note: "Mereka" means both 'they' and 'their' in Indonesian; unlike English, it doesn't change form based on grammatical role.

sentences.text: Mereka makan nasi di warung bersama.
sentences.en: They eat rice together at a small restaurant.

sentences.text: Rumah mereka dekat pantai Bali.
sentences.en: Their house is near the Bali beach.

sentences.text: Mereka pergi ke pasar setiap pagi.
sentences.en: They go to the market every morning.

english: to do the cooking, to cook (something)
note: "Masak" means to cook; note that "masak" can also mean "really?/seriously?" in informal speech, so context matters.

sentences.text: Ibu masak nasi goreng di dapur.
sentences.en: Mom cooks fried rice in the kitchen.

sentences.text: Saya ingin masak mie untuk makan malam.
sentences.en: I want to cook noodles for dinner.

sentences.text: Hari ini kamu masak apa?
sentences.en: What are you cooking today?

note: "Membantu" is the formal/full form; "bantu" is the casual base form — both mean 'to help'; often confused with "tolong" which is used to request help.

sentences.text: Saya membantu ibu di dapur.
sentences.en: I help my mother in the kitchen.

sentences.text: Dia bantu saya membawa tas berat.
sentences.en: He helps me carry the heavy bag.

sentences.text: Kami membantu turis yang tersesat.
sentences.en: We help the tourist who is lost.

note: 'Mandi' means to bathe or shower; used for both baths and showers, unlike English which distinguishes them.

sentences.text: Saya mandi setiap pagi di rumah.
sentences.en: I shower every morning at home.

sentences.text: Dia mandi dua kali sehari.
sentences.en: She showers twice a day.

sentences.text: Anak itu belum mandi hari ini.
sentences.en: That child has not bathed today.

note: 'Prihatin' means deeply concerned or troubled; more formal/emotional than 'khawatir' (worried); often used about social or community issues.

sentences.text: Saya prihatin dengan sampah di pantai ini.
sentences.en: I am very concerned about the trash on this beach.

sentences.text: Ibu prihatin dengan kesehatan anak itu.
sentences.en: Mother is very concerned about that child's health.

english: vegetables, a variety of vegetables, all sorts of vegetables
note: 'sayur-sayuran' is the reduplicated plural of 'sayur' (vegetable), used informally to mean 'all kinds of vegetables'; more general than naming a specific vegetable.

sentences.text: Ibu membeli sayur-sayuran di pasar setiap hari.
sentences.en: Mom buys vegetables at the market every day.

sentences.text: Anak-anak harus makan sayur-sayuran supaya sehat.
sentences.en: Children must eat vegetables to stay healthy.

sentences.text: Warung itu menjual sayur-sayuran yang segar.
sentences.en: That small stall sells fresh vegetables.

note: 'Sedang' marks an action in progress (like English '-ing'); it sits before the verb and is used in everyday casual speech — don't confuse it with 'sedang' meaning 'medium/moderate'.

sentences.text: Saya sedang makan nasi goreng sekarang.
sentences.en: I am eating fried rice right now.

sentences.text: Ibu sedang memasak di dapur.
sentences.en: Mom is cooking in the kitchen.

sentences.text: Mereka sedang belajar bahasa Indonesia.
sentences.en: They are studying Indonesian.

english: to sleep, to go to bed
note: 'Tidur' means to sleep or go to bed; commonly confused with 'istirahat' (to rest); related words: 'mengantuk' (sleepy), 'bangun' (to wake up).

sentences.text: Saya mau tidur sekarang.
sentences.en: I want to sleep now.

sentences.text: Anak itu tidur di kamar.
sentences.en: That child is sleeping in the room.

sentences.text: Dia tidur pukul sembilan malam.
sentences.en: She goes to bed at nine at night.

english: how much is the price of...?
note: Used to ask the price of something; informal and very common in markets and shops; related: 'harga' (price), 'berapa' (how much/many).

sentences.text: Berapa harga nasi goreng ini?
sentences.en: How much is the price of this fried rice?

sentences.text: Berapa harga kaos di toko itu?
sentences.en: How much is the price of the shirt in that shop?

sentences.text: Berapa harga oleh-oleh di pasar?
sentences.en: How much is the price of souvenirs at the market?

note: 'Botol' means bottle; commonly used for water bottles ('botol air') or any container bottle; related: 'gelas' (glass/cup), 'cangkir' (mug).

sentences.text: Saya minum air dari botol ini.
sentences.en: I drink water from this bottle.

sentences.text: Tolong beli satu botol air mineral.
sentences.en: Please buy one bottle of mineral water.

sentences.text: Botol itu ada di meja.
sentences.en: That bottle is on the table.

note: 'Bunga' means both 'flower' and 'interest rate' (on loans/savings); beginners often first learn the 'flower' meaning, but the financial meaning is very common in everyday banking contexts.

sentences.text: Saya membeli bunga di pasar pagi.
sentences.en: I bought flowers at the morning market.

sentences.text: Bunga tabungan saya tiga persen.
sentences.en: My savings interest rate is three percent.

sentences.text: Bunga mawar itu sangat cantik.
sentences.en: That rose flower is very beautiful.

note: 'Cari apa?' is informal/casual Indonesian for 'what are you looking for?'; common in markets and shops; related: 'mencari' (to look for), 'mau cari apa?' (what do you want to look for?)

sentences.text: Kak, cari apa di pasar ini?
sentences.en: Sis/Bro, what are you looking for at this market?

sentences.text: Bu, cari apa di toko ini?
sentences.en: Ma'am, what are you looking for in this store?

sentences.text: Hei, kamu cari apa di sini?
sentences.en: Hey, what are you looking for here?

note: 'Harga' means price or cost of something; commonly used in markets and shops; related words: 'mahal' (expensive), 'murah' (cheap), 'berapa' (how much).

sentences.text: Berapa harga nasi goreng ini?
sentences.en: How much is the price of this fried rice?

sentences.text: Harga buah di pasar sangat murah.
sentences.en: The price of fruit at the market is very cheap.

sentences.text: Saya tanya harga kamar hotel itu.
sentences.en: I asked the price of that hotel room.

note: 'Harganya' means 'the price is' or 'it costs'; formed from 'harga' (price) + '-nya' (the/its); often confused with just 'harga' which is the noun alone.

sentences.text: Berapa harganya nasi goreng ini?
sentences.en: How much does this fried rice cost?

sentences.text: Harganya dua puluh ribu rupiah.
sentences.en: It costs twenty thousand rupiah.

sentences.text: Harganya murah sekali di pasar.
sentences.en: It costs very cheap at the market.

note: 'Jam' means clock/watch, hour, and o'clock all in one — e.g. 'jam tiga' means '3 o'clock' or 'three hours'; don't confuse with 'waktu' (time in general).

sentences.text: Sekarang jam berapa?
sentences.en: What time is it now?

sentences.text: Toko itu buka jam sembilan pagi.
sentences.en: That shop opens at nine in the morning.

sentences.text: Saya belajar dua jam setiap hari.
sentences.en: I study for two hours every day.

note: 'Kursi' means chair; not to be confused with 'meja' (table); also used in phrases like 'kursi roda' (wheelchair).

sentences.text: Tolong ambilkan kursi untuk tamu itu.
sentences.en: Please get a chair for that guest.

sentences.text: Kursi ini sangat nyaman untuk duduk.
sentences.en: This chair is very comfortable to sit on.

sentences.text: Ada dua kursi di ruang tamu.
sentences.en: There are two chairs in the living room.

note: "Kursi malas" literally means 'lazy chair' and refers to a recliner or easy chair; often confused with 'kursi goyang' (rocking chair), but they are different furniture items.

sentences.text: Ayah duduk di kursi malas setiap sore.
sentences.en: Dad sits in the easy chair every afternoon.

sentences.text: Kursi malas itu sangat nyaman untuk bersantai.
sentences.en: That easy chair is very comfortable for relaxing.

sentences.text: Kami punya kursi malas di ruang tamu.
sentences.en: We have an easy chair in the living room.

note: "Kursi panjang" literally means 'long chair' and refers to a lounge chair or sofa; beginners may confuse it with "sofa" (also used in Indonesian) or "bangku" (bench).

sentences.text: Saya duduk di kursi panjang itu.
sentences.en: I sit on that lounge chair.

sentences.text: Kursi panjang di ruang tamu baru.
sentences.en: The sofa in the living room is new.

sentences.text: Ibu tidur di kursi panjang merah.
sentences.en: Mom is sleeping on the red lounge chair.

note: "Kompor" refers to any stovetop or small portable/benchtop gas burner, very common in Indonesian kitchens; not to be confused with "oven" (oven) which bakes enclosed.

sentences.text: Ibu memasak nasi di atas kompor.
sentences.en: Mum is cooking rice on the stove.

sentences.text: Tolong matikan kompor setelah selesai masak.
sentences.en: Please turn off the stove after cooking.

sentences.text: Kompor di dapur kami pakai gas.
sentences.en: The stove in our kitchen uses gas.

note: 'Lampu' means lamp or light; used for any electric light; related words: 'lampu tidur' (night light), 'lampu jalan' (street light).

sentences.text: Tolong nyalakan lampu di kamar ini.
sentences.en: Please turn on the light in this room.

sentences.text: Lampu di sini sangat terang.
sentences.en: The lamp here is very bright.

sentences.text: Saya membeli lampu baru kemarin.
sentences.en: I bought a new lamp yesterday.

note: 'Lemari' means cupboard or wardrobe; 'lemari pakaian' is a clothes wardrobe, 'lemari es' is a refrigerator — a common compound to know.

sentences.text: Baju saya ada di dalam lemari.
sentences.en: My clothes are inside the cupboard.

sentences.text: Tolong tutup pintu lemari itu.
sentences.en: Please close the cupboard door.

sentences.text: Lemari ini sangat besar dan baru.
sentences.en: This cupboard is very big and new.

note: 'Lemari es' (literally 'ice cupboard') is the standard everyday term; 'kulkas' (from Dutch 'koelkast') is equally common and often preferred in casual speech.

sentences.text: Tolong simpan susu itu di lemari es.
sentences.en: Please put that milk in the fridge.

sentences.text: Lemari es kami penuh dengan buah-buahan.
sentences.en: Our fridge is full of fruits.

sentences.text: Ada air dingin di lemari es.
sentences.en: There is cold water in the fridge.

note: 'Lemari pakaian' literally means 'clothes cabinet'; used for wardrobe or closet, not to be confused with 'lemari es' (refrigerator).

sentences.text: Baju saya ada di lemari pakaian.
sentences.en: My clothes are in the wardrobe.

sentences.text: Lemari pakaian di kamar saya besar.
sentences.en: The wardrobe in my room is big.

sentences.text: Dia menyimpan baju di lemari pakaian.
sentences.en: She keeps her clothes in the wardrobe.

note: 'Meja makan' literally means 'eating table'; 'meja' alone means any table, so context matters — related words include 'kursi makan' (dining chair) and 'ruang makan' (dining room).

sentences.text: Kami makan bersama di meja makan.
sentences.en: We eat together at the dining table.

sentences.text: Tolong taruh piring di meja makan.
sentences.en: Please put the plate on the dining table.

sentences.text: Meja makan kami besar dan baru.
